Each patch carries a hidden class label y v y_{v} and three embeddings: (1) 𝐟 v \mathbf{f}_{v} from a VLM, (2) 𝐠 v \mathbf{g}_{v} from a second purely visual encoder, and (3) 𝐟 k , v \mathbf{f}_{k,v} representing the k t ​ h k^{th} biological features extracted from the patch. These hidden variables are used to define the CRF objective function to minimize [ 5 , 6 ] : f ⁡ ( 𝐲 ) = ∑ v ∈ 𝒱 ϕ v ​ ( y v ) ⏟ unary ​ Φ u + ∑ ( v , w ) ∈ ℰ Φ v ​ w ​ ( y v , y w ) ⏟ pairwise ​ Φ p , f(\mathbf{y})\;=\;\underbrace{\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\phi_{v}(y_{v})}_{\text{unary }\Phi_{u}}\;+\;\underbrace{\sum_{(v,w)\in\mathcal{E}}\Phi_{vw}(y_{v},y_{w})}_{\text{pairwise }\Phi_{p}}, (1) where 𝐲 \mathbf{y} is the label distribution. The unary potential penalizes assigning a label that is a poor match based on its own embedding, while the pairwise potential Φ v ​ w \Phi_{vw} penalizes assigning an incompatible pair of labels to two connected patches, thereby encouraging consistency across patches. The objective function in Eq. ( 1 ) is minimized approximately via mean-field inference [ 15 ] , which restricts the solution to a product of independent per-vertex marginals Q ⁡ ( 𝐲 ) = ∏ v Q v ​ ( y v ) Q(\mathbf{y})=\prod_{v}Q_{v}(y_{v}) . This yields an iterative update in which each marginal Q v Q_{v} is recomputed as the exponential of minus the unary potential ϕ v \phi_{v} combined with the pairwise potentials Φ v ​ w \Phi_{vw} , each averaged over the neighbor’s current marginal Q w Q_{w} rather than its unknown true label.

Repeating this update at every vertex in turn implements message passing along the graph 𝒢 \mathcal{G} : each patch’s marginal is recomputed from its neighbors’ current marginals, for a fixed number of propagation rounds. 2.2 Unary potential As in [ 5 ] , the unary potential requires no task-specific training: a VLM encodes each patch into a visual embedding 𝐟 v \mathbf{f}_{v} and each class l l into a textual embedding 𝐭 l \mathbf{t}_{l} (averaged over a set of prompts). The unary potential is then defined based on the cosine similiarity: ϕ v ​ ( y v = l ) = − log ⁡ softmax l ⁡ ( 𝐟 v ​ 𝐭 l ⊤ ∥ 𝐟 v ∥ ​ ∥ 𝐭 l ∥ ) . \phi_{v}(y_{v}=l)\;=\;-\log\operatorname{softmax}_{l}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{f}_{v}\mathbf{t}_{l}^{\top}}{\lVert\mathbf{f}_{v}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{t}_{l}\rVert}\right). We keep unchanged the two pairwise terms introduced by HistoCRF [ 5 ] . The diversity term connects each patch v v to its | 𝒩 v | |\mathcal{N}_{v}| most dissimilar patches, the similarity being defined by: sim = 𝐠 v ​ 𝐠 l ⊤ ∥ 𝐠 v ∥ ​ ∥ 𝐠 l ∥ . \operatorname{sim}=\frac{\mathbf{g}_{v}\mathbf{g}_{l}^{\top}}{\lVert\mathbf{g}_{v}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{g}_{l}\rVert}. (3) This term penalizes assigning the same label to dissimilar patches, so predictions do not collapse onto a single class: φ v ​ w ​ ( y v , y w ) = δ y v , y w ​ ( 1 − sim ⁡ ( 𝐠 v , 𝐠 w ) ) . \varphi_{vw}(y_{v},y_{w})\;=\;\delta_{y_{v},y_{w}}\bigl(1-\operatorname{sim}(\mathbf{g}_{v},\mathbf{g}_{w})\bigr). (4) Let 𝒜 \mathcal{A} be the set of annotated patches. The annotation term connects each annotated patch v ∈ 𝒜 v\in\mathcal{A} to its | ℳ v | |\mathcal{M}_{v}| most similar patches. This term penalizes assigning them different labels, propagating expert supervision to visually related patches: ψ v ​ w ​ ( y v , y w ) = ( 1 − δ y v , y w ) ​ sim ⁡ ( 𝐠 v , 𝐠 w ) .

\psi_{vw}(y_{v},y_{w})\;=\;(1-\delta_{y_{v},y_{w}})\operatorname{sim}(\mathbf{g}_{v},\mathbf{g}_{w}). (5) Biological term. SlideCRF [ 6 ] extends this pairwise potential with biological terms, composed of texture and color cues. This term takes the same form as Eq. ( 5 ) to penalize patches with similar biological features f k \textbf{f}_{k} to have different labels, the similarity being defined by a Gaussian kernel applied to the Euclidean distance between the features extracted from each patch: sim 2 ​ ( 𝐟 k , v , 𝐟 k , w ) = exp ​ ( − ‖ 𝐟 k , v − 𝐟 k , w ‖ 2 2 ​ σ 2 ) . \text{sim}_{2}(\mathbf{f}_{k,v},\mathbf{f}_{k,w})=\text{exp}\left(-\frac{||\mathbf{f}_{k,v}-\mathbf{f}_{k,w}||^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right). (6) Unlike SlideCRF, we combine any subset of biological cue { f 1 , … , f K } \{f_{1},\dots,f_{K}\} into a single pairwise term where each cue is divided by its own average magnitude mean ⁡ ( ξ k ) \operatorname{mean}(\xi_{k}) so a larger raw scale cannot dominate: ξ v ​ w = 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K ξ k , v ​ w mean ⁡ ( ξ k ) , \displaystyle\xi_{vw}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\xi_{k,vw}}{\operatorname{mean}(\xi_{k})}, (7) ξ k , v ​ w = ( 1 − δ y v , y w ) ​ sim 2 ⁡ ( 𝐟 k , v , 𝐟 k , w ) . \displaystyle\xi_{k,vw}=(1-\delta_{y_{v},y_{w}})\operatorname{sim}_{2}(\mathbf{f}_{k,v},\mathbf{f}_{k,w}). We choose May-Grünwald-Giemsa staining and chromatin texture (cf. Section 3.1) for the final set of cues. Another difference with SlideCRF is that each patch v v is connected to its | ℳ v | |\mathcal{M}_{v}| similar patches based on their embedding (Eq. ( 3 )). Final pairwise potential.

CytoCRF correctly identifies the proliferative-follicular region, correcting the colloid misclassification of the KEEP zero-shot prediction, all while maintaining correct red blood cells predictions. Datasets. We evaluate on 10 cytology-oriented, patch-level classification datasets covering cervical (BMT [ 27 ] , APACC [ 17 ] , SIPaKMeD [ 21 ] , MLCC [ 9 ] , HiCervix [ 1 ] , Herlev [ 11 ] ), breast (FNAC [ 23 ] ), blood (BloodMNIST [ 29 ] ), body-cavity fluid (BCFC [ 24 ] ), and bone marrow cells (BMCD [ 25 ] ). Unless stated otherwise, we report the balanced accuracy of the final mean-field inference, averaged over 10 seeds per dataset and then over the 10 datasets. Foundation models. As unary 𝐟 v \mathbf{f}_{v} candidates, PLIP [ 8 ] , CONCH [ 18 ] , Quilt-B16 [ 10 ] and KEEP [ 31 ] , with eight vision-only encoders as pairwise 𝐠 v \mathbf{g}_{v} candidates, including the visual encoder of the four VLMs, GigaPath [ 28 ] , UNI [ 2 ] , DinoBloom [ 14 ] and UniCAS [ 12 ] . Biological cues. We test two color and three texture cues, one from SlideCRF’s own implementation. The feature he [ 22 ] deconvolves the patch into the hematoxylin eosin space and concatenates the mean and standard deviation of each stain channel; mgg does the same with a May-Grünwald-Giemsa matrix, better suited to cytology than the histological he stain.

texture [ 7 , 19 ] concatenates gray-level co-occurrence statistics with a local binary pattern histogram of the grayscale patch; chrom applies the same statistics to the nucleus-stain channel; density thresholds (Otsu) that channel into a nucleus mask and computes its area fraction, a nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio proxy, and its spatial variance. Annotation strategy. random uniformly samples patches; error selects patches where the model’s current prediction disagrees with the ground-truth label, simulating a pathologist correcting the model’s mistakes; and oscillation selects patches whose predicted label flips most often across the mean-field propagation steps of the previous round. 3.2 CytoCRF outperforms existing CRF frameworks Table 1 reports balanced accuracy averaged over our ten cytology datasets for our base configuration: we combine the color cue mgg with the texture cue chrom , and use KEEP for the unary potential and DinoBloom for the pairwise potential. We compare it against ZS predictions and two CRF baselines: HistoCRF-style (diversity and annotation terms only) and SlideCRF-style (addition of the texture and he cues, with a dissimilar graph). ZS classification with KEEP VLM reaches only 26.7% balanced accuracy. Our configuration leads at every budget (41.2–60.0%), and its margin over HistoCRF-style grows rather than shrinks as more annotations are added (+5.8pp at budget 5 to +13.6pp at budget 50), showing that the gain from our biological pairwise term compounds with more supervision instead of being absorbed by it. SlideCRF-style, run on its own historical dissimilar graph, only overtakes ZS from budget 10 onward and remains the weakest CRF configuration throughout. Figure 1 illustrates CytoCRF qualitatively on a real WSI image. 3.3 Ablation experiments Unary and pairwise potentials.

Table 2 reports the full grid crossing the four unary VLM candidates 𝐟 v \mathbf{f}_{v} and the eight pairwise visual encoder candidates 𝐠 v \mathbf{g}_{v} , each evaluated with our base configuration ( mgg and chrom ). The pairwise encoder matters far more than the unary VLM: DinoBloom is the best pairwise choice for every unary candidate and Quilt-B16 the worst, a gap of over 14pp regardless of the unary VLM. The four vision-only encoders (UNI, GigaPath, DinoBloom, UniCAS) also consistently outperform the four VLMs’ own vision encoder as pairwise candidates, confirming that a dedicated visual encoder captures finer-grained patch similarity than a VLM’s vision encoder. KEEP paired with DinoBloom reaches the best overall balanced accuracy. ( 7 ) at equal weight over the similar neighborhood graph. chrom is the strongest solo cue and mgg + chrom the strongest pair; the five solo cues are otherwise close. We also ablate the neighborhood graph itself: switching SlideCRF’s dissimilar to the similar graph improves balanced accuracy by 20pp (34.6–54.7%). Neighbors from 𝐠 v \mathbf{g}_{v} are thus more informative than either alternative graph. This holds beyond solo cues: our default pair mgg + chrom reaches 55.3% on similar versus 43.9%/43.8% on mgg ’s or chrom ’s own raw-feature graph, and chrom alone reaches 54.4% versus 36.2% on dissimilar. Pairwise graph ensemble. Beyond the single KEEP and DinoBloom graph, we test enlarging the set of dissimilar 𝒩 v \mathcal{N}_{v} and similar ℳ v \mathcal{M}_{v} patches with the neighbors found in one or two additional FMs’ own embedding spaces. The potential itself is still computed from 𝐠 v \mathbf{g}_{v} (DinoBloom): only the set of candidate neighbors grows, increasing the relations between patches. Each additional FM brings a further gain, from +1.35pp for KEEP to +3.10pp for KEEP and GigaPath, with no saturation across the three configurations tested. Annotation strategy. Finally, we compare our three annotation strategies (Sec. 3.1 ) for our default configuration ( mgg + chrom on KEEP + DinoBloom), over R ∈ { 1 , 2 , 5 , 10 , 15 , 20 , 25 } R\in\{1,2,5,10,15,20,25\} human-in-the-loop rounds of 5 5 annotations each (Figure 2 ).

Correcting the model’s wrong patches ( error ) is an oracle upper bound on what a human-in-the-loop protocol could gain as it relies on the ground truth label. At the smallest budget (5 annotations, a single round with no propagation history yet to exploit), the three strategies are within 1.2pp of each other. From 50 to 100 annotations, random and oscillation have performances close to each other. The gains from oscillation do not increase until 125 annotations, suggesting that its signal requires more propagation rounds to become reliable. 3.1 Experimental setup Figure 1: Qualitative illustration of CytoCRF on a thyroid fine-needle aspiration cytology slide. The gains from oscillation do not increase until 125 annotations, suggesting that its signal requires more propagation rounds to become reliable. 4 Conclusion We adapted a CRF-based refinement of vision-language model predictions to cytology, replacing the spatial neighborhood assumption of prior whole-slide work with a systematic search over FM pairs and biological/color cues suited to independent cytology patch collections.

On ten cytology datasets, CytoCRF beats both existing CRF-based baselines at every annotation budget we tested, with the margin widening rather than narrowing as more annotations become available. Combining the pairwise neighborhood across additional FMs brings a further, uncorrelated gain that does not saturate within the range we tested. Together these results show that domain-specific care in choosing the graph, not just the pairwise term, is what makes CRF refinement work on cytology’s patch-independent, multi-stain benchmarks. In every ablation we ran, the neighborhood topology itself, whether set by the pairwise FM, the similar/dissimilar graph, or the multi-FM ensemble, mattered more than any change to the potentials computed over it. A natural direction for future work is therefore to study this topology directly, for instance by learning or adapting the neighborhood structure rather than fixing it to a handful of hand-picked FMs and similarity thresholds.
